title: Fiber: targets, sources, and why it helps fat loss
chunks: Fiber is the part of plant carbohydrates your body cannot fully digest. It does not provide much usable energy, but it does a lot of useful work: it slows digestion, steadies blood sugar, feeds healthy gut bacteria, supports regular bowel movements, and keeps you full on fewer calories.

Aim for about 25–38 g of fiber per day, or roughly 14 g per 1,000 kcal. Many people fall well short of this. Increasing fiber is one of the simplest ways to feel more satisfied during a calorie deficit without adding many calories.

Great fiber sources include vegetables, fruit (especially berries, apples, and pears with skin), legumes (beans, lentils, chickpeas), oats, whole grains, nuts, seeds, and potatoes with skin. Building meals around these gives you fiber, micronutrients, and volume at once.

There are two types: soluble fiber (in oats, beans, apples, chia) forms a gel that slows digestion and helps satiety and cholesterol, while insoluble fiber (in whole grains, vegetables, skins) adds bulk and supports regularity. A varied whole-food diet naturally provides both.

Increase fiber gradually and drink enough water. Jumping from a low-fiber diet to a very high one overnight can cause bloating and gas. Add 5 g or so at a time over a couple of weeks and let your gut adjust.

High-volume, high-fiber foods are a powerful tool when cutting: a large salad, a bowl of vegetables, or a serving of beans fills your stomach for relatively few calories, which makes a deficit far easier to sustain.
If you have a diagnosed digestive condition such as IBS or IBD, your fiber needs and tolerances may differ — work with your doctor or a registered dietitian rather than following general targets.
